title: How evidence-based is the “hashtag ADHD test” (#adhdtest). A cross-sectional content analysis of TikTok videos on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) screening
screen_reason: A quantitative share with a denominator IS reported (46/50, 92% of videos 'misleading'), so the paper is not screened out for lack of a usable number — but the numerator is defined by concordance with the ASRS-v1.1 screener (≥4 of 6 items present = 'useful', otherwise 'misleading'), not by any judgement of truth or falsity against a ground truth. Per §3 the rows are therefore coded construct=QUALITY and kept for the appendix only, excluded from prevalence. If the review's convention is to screen QUALITY-only papers as EXCLUDE outright, flip this to EXCLUDE with the ground 'quality-only: completeness-against-ASRS, not veracity' and drop both rows — nothing else in the paper changes that call.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language TikTok videos; authors based in New Zealand)
estimates.date: Videos identified and coded on a single day, 24 December 2023; no date limit on the videos themselves
estimates.measure_type: % of the top 50 #adhdtest TikTok videos classified “misleading” (i.e. containing fewer than 4 of the 6 ASRS-v1.1 screener questions)
estimates.denominator: 50 top #adhdtest TikTok videos sorted by relevance, English-language, describing an ADHD test or diagnosis
estimates.definition: Video labelled “misleading” if its content did NOT include at least 4 of the 6 ASRS-v1.1 screener questions
estimates.misinfo_def: No veracity definition is given: a video is “useful” if “its contents had at least 4 out of the 6 questions on the ASRS-v1.1 screener” and “otherwise, they were labelled as misleading”
estimates.source_quote: Out of the 50 included #adhdtest videos, 92% (n = 46) were misleading.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract — Result, p. 82; same figure in Result, 'The content analysis of the uploaded videos into useful and misleading — Prevalence', p. 84
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Both authors — SV, a psychiatry trainee registrar, and SS, a specialist adult psychiatrist with experience in adult ADHD assessment — watched each video and compared its content with the WHO Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1) 6-item screener; a video was 'useful' if ≥4 of the 6 screener questions were present, 'misleading' otherwise. Agreement reported as complete (“there was no disagreement between the two for the classification of the selected fifty videos”); no kappa.
estimates.moderator_quote: The videos were categorized as “useful” if its contents had at least 4 out of the 6 screening questions of the ASRS-v1.1 screener which is needed for screening positive for ADHD assessment; otherwise, they were labelled as misleading.
estimates.notes: CONSTRUCT: QUALITY, not CONTENT, and this is the exact case §3 names — the label 'misleading' means 'covers fewer than 4 of the 6 ASRS-v1.1 screener items', a completeness/concordance criterion, so a video that says nothing false at all (e.g. an accurate personal account, or a correct partial description of ADHD) is counted as misleading. No item was judged against any external ground truth for truth or falsity. The row is kept per §3 but must be excluded from prevalence. The descriptive content of the flagged videos (ASMR 'tests', dot tests, funnel tests, SPECT-scan claims) does suggest many really are false, but the paper gives no share coded that way, so the 92% cannot be re-read as a falsity rate. Country coded Global: no country restriction is stated, only English language and no logged-in account. [quote check, this pass] The results-section wording (“Out of the 50 selected videos, useful videos amounted to 8% (n = 4), while 92% (n = 46) were misleading videos”) is broken by an end-of-line hyphenation of 'mis-leading' in the v2txt rendering, so the identical abstract sentence, which is contiguous, is quoted instead.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language TikTok videos; authors based in New Zealand)
estimates.date: Engagement metadata collected on a single day, 24 December 2023
estimates.measure_type: % of all likes on the 50 sampled #adhdtest videos that accrued to videos classified “misleading”
estimates.value_raw: Misleading videos: 96% of the total likes, 99% of the total comments, 93% of the total favorites (totals: 10,492,332 likes, 819,261 comments, 1,301,611 favorites); useful videos 4% / 1% / 7%
estimates.denominator: 10,492,332 likes received in total by the 50 sampled #adhdtest videos as of 24 December 2023
estimates.definition: Likes on videos labelled “misleading” (fewer than 4 of the 6 ASRS-v1.1 screener questions present), as a share of all likes on the 50 sampled videos
estimates.misinfo_def: No veracity definition is given: a video is “useful” if “its contents had at least 4 out of the 6 questions on the ASRS-v1.1 screener” and “otherwise, they were labelled as misleading”
estimates.source_quote: Misleading videos were more engaging compared to the useful videos, with 96% of the total likes, 99% of the total comments, and 93% of the total favorites. Compared to that the useful videos had only 4% of the total likes, 1% of the total comments, and 7% of the total favorites.
estimates.page_loc: Result — 'TikTok user engagement with selected useful and misleading videos', p. 84; Table 3, p. 86
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Both authors — SV, a psychiatry trainee registrar, and SS, a specialist adult psychiatrist with experience in adult ADHD assessment — watched each video and compared its content with the WHO Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1) 6-item screener; a video was 'useful' if ≥4 of the 6 screener questions were present, 'misleading' otherwise. Agreement reported as complete (“there was no disagreement between the two for the classification of the selected fifty videos”); no kappa.
estimates.moderator_quote: On 24/12/23, the selected top 50 #adhdtest videos had a total of 10492332 likes, 819261 comments, and 1301611 favorites.
estimates.notes: Under the denominator rule (§3) a share of engagement would be SHARING/content_share, but the 'misleading' label is a completeness score, so QUALITY governs the row and it must stay out of prevalence AND out of any sharing analysis. Kept because it is a distinct, verbatim measure an adjudicator may want. value_pct uses the likes figure as the representative engagement metric; the comments (99%) and favorites (93%) shares are in value_raw. unit='item' is the least-bad fit — the counted objects are likes, which the schema has no unit for. Note the denominator is only these 50 videos, so this is not a platform-wide engagement share.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) The typology of the misleading videos — ASMR 63% (n=29), miscellaneous 24% (n=11), dot test 13% (n=6) — are shares of the 46 misleading videos, i.e. within-misinformation composition (R3), and would need within_misinfo_content=true; they add nothing to prevalence, so no row. (2) 'Amongst all selected videos, ASMR engaged the users the most with 49% of the likes, 55% of the comments, and 34% of the total favorites' — a within-category engagement split, same reason. (3) Mean engagement counts and their p values (Table 3: mean likes 219,508 for misleading vs 98,738 for useful, p=.229; mean comments 17,621 vs 2177, p=.008; favorites p=.885) are means, not shares. (4) The 52% of top-100 ADHD TikTok videos found misleading by Yeung et al. (2022) is a figure the paper cites from elsewhere — barred by R8. (5) No country, no date window and no sampling frame beyond 'sorted by relevance' on one day are reported, and the top-50 cut is rank-truncated: the 92% describes the head of one hashtag on one day, not ADHD content on TikTok. OCR note: the text has ligature damage ('ﬁ' runs, spaced digits like 'n = 4'), but every extracted number appears twice (abstract and results, or results and table) and is unambiguous.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of the top 50 English-language TikTok videos returned for the hashtag #adhdtest, sorted by relevance with no date limit, searched in the mobile app without an account to limit algorithmic personalisation, screened and collected on a single day (24 December 2023); each video watched and compared with the ASRS-v1.1 6-item screener first by a psychiatry trainee registrar and then by a specialist adult psychiatrist, with categories 'useful' (≥4/6 items) vs 'misleading'; complete agreement reported between the two raters but no kappa; engagement metadata (likes, comments, favourites) captured the same day; descriptive statistics and mean comparisons. Authors' stated limitations: single-day scoping and English only, so it does not generalise to TikTok content overall.
rob.item6_quote: The videos were categorized as “useful” if its contents had at least 4 out of the 6 questions on the ASRS-v1.1 screener.
rob.item10_quote: Out of the 50 selected videos, useful videos amounted to 8% ( n = 4), while 92% ( n = 46) were misleading videos.
